title: The Library and the Night: Buenos Aires to Geneva
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Buenos Aires, the Library of the Father

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the house on Calle Tucumán
stops.campa: Jorge Francisco Isidoro Luis Borges is born on the fourth floor of a house on Calle Tucumán, in the small hours before dawn, the first child of Jorge Guillermo Borges, lawyer and sometime lecturer in psychology, and Leonor Acevedo Suárez, of old criollo military stock. English runs in the blood on the father's side: the grandmother, Frances Haslam, came out from Staffordshire and never lost her tongue. The house will later be torn down; the district remembers only a bronze plaque. The child inherits, unknown to anyone yet, the retina that has already begun to fail in generations before him.
suggested_refs: The birthplace plaque on Calle Tucumán, Buenos Aires, marking the house since demolished
sources: Fundación Internacional Jorge Luis Borges, biographical chronology

stops.name: Palermo, the paternal library
stops.campa: The family's rented house in Palermo has a walled garden his mother will later call the first labyrinth, and beyond the dining room a library of English books floor to ceiling: his father's, unabridged, unlocked to the boy. Jorge Guillermo, half-blind already, cannot read them himself for many hours at a stretch and gives them instead to his son, who reads Stevenson, Twain, and Dickens, and — before he ever opens it in Spanish — an English Don Quixote, so that for years he believes chivalry a foreign invention. He will say, decades on, that no other event in his life mattered more.
stops.quote: If I were asked to name the chief event in my life, I should say my father's library.
stops.quote_source: An Autobiographical Essay, The New Yorker, 1970
suggested_refs: The family library of Jorge Guillermo Borges, English-language shelf, Palermo, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the sailing of the Sierra Nevada
stops.campa: On the third of February the whole household — Jorge Guillermo, Leonor, the two children, and the maternal grandmother — boards the German steamer Sierra Nevada, bound by way of Lisbon and Paris for Geneva, where a Swiss oculist has been named the last hope against the father's advancing blindness. No one on the dock imagines the crossing will be for good; Europe is at peace and the visit is meant to last a season. The father carries the family's darkening inheritance in his eyes; the son, not yet fifteen, carries a satchel of English books and does not yet know he carries the same darkness.
suggested_refs: The Hamburg-line steamer Sierra Nevada, the family's crossing to Lisbon and Paris, February 1914
sources: María Esther Vázquez, Borges: esplendor y derrota (1996)

segments.name: Geneva, the War and the Schoolroom

stops.name: Geneva, rue de Malagnou
stops.campa: The family takes rooms at Malagnou 17, meaning to stay a season for the father's treatment; within months the guns open on the Marne and the border to France and Germany closes around them. Geneva becomes home for five years no one planned. The boy, not yet fifteen and already reading Carlyle in English on the shores of the lake, watches the neutral city fill with refugees, spies, and the exiled of every warring nation, and begins, without noticing the hinge turning, to become a citizen of books before he is a citizen of any one country.
suggested_refs: 17 rue de Malagnou, Eaux-Vives, Geneva, the family's wartime address

stops.name: Geneva, the Collège Calvin
stops.campa: Enrolled at the Collège Calvin in the old town, Jorge Luis takes his Latin and his French among Genevan boys who tease him at first for his accent and his foreignness, and who come, within a term, to respect the strange South American who has read more than the masters. He labors over Latin declensions with real difficulty and real devotion; French opens easily, almost by osmosis, from the streets and the classroom both. He will say the city gave him more than any single teacher could have — a whole grammar of Europe entered through a schoolboy's satchel.
stops.quote: A Ginebra le debo la revelación del francés, del latín, del alemán, del expresionismo, de Schopenhauer, de la doctrina de Buddha, del taoísmo, de Conrad, de Lafcadio Hearn y de la nostalgia de Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: The Collège Calvin in Geneva's old town, where Borges took his baccalauréat

stops.name: Geneva, Schopenhauer, Heine, and the Golem
stops.campa: Restless with the school's pace, the boy teaches himself German by the brute method of reading Heine with a dictionary at his elbow, then goes on unaided into Schopenhauer's Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung, a system that will outlast every other philosophy in his private canon. In these same months he comes on Gustav Meyrink's new novel Der Golem, the tale of the clay giant animated by a word hidden in its mouth. Kabbalah enters his imagination here first, as a German expressionist nightmare, years before he meets it again in Madrid as a discipline of hermeneutics and letters.
suggested_refs: Gustav Meyrink's Der Golem (1915), read by Borges in Geneva

stops.name: Geneva, the baccalauréat
stops.campa: The Collège Calvin grants him his baccalauréat in the summer, four years and a war after the family meant only to pass a season in the city. Peace has not yet been signed and the borders south are still closed by influenza and troop movements; the family will wait almost a year more before they can leave for the warmer country his father's lungs and eyes both need. Behind him the boy leaves a schoolboy's German and a schoolboy's Latin, and a permanent, lifelong debt to a city he will one day choose, over all others, to die in.
suggested_refs: The diploma of the Collège Calvin, class of 1918

stops.name: Valldemossa and Palma, Mallorca
stops.campa: The family crosses to Barcelona and within weeks to the island, where they pass most of a year between Palma and the hill village of Valldemossa, guests of the Sureda family in their old stone house above the terraces. Here Jorge Luis, not yet twenty, forms a close and lettered friendship with Jacobo Sureda, and the two draft manifestos for a poetic school that exists mostly on paper and in their correspondence. The Mediterranean light after the Genevan winters feels, he will say, like a second and gentler revelation. He writes his first serious verse on this island and burns most of it within the year.
stops.quote: hace unos quince días abandonamos la Ciudad Condal para venir a pasar el verano a las Islas Baleares
suggested_refs: The Sureda family's house at Valldemossa, Mallorca, where the Borges family lodged
sources: comounlibro.com, 'Jorge Luis Borges en España. El Ultraísmo'

stops.name: Seville, "Himno al mar"
stops.campa: On the last day of the year the Sevillian magazine Grecia prints "Himno al mar," dedicated to the poet Adriano del Valle: the first appearance in print of anything Borges has written. He will later call it an attempt, with all his young strength, to be Walt Whitman, and will disown and eventually destroy the little book of "red psalms" it belonged to. But the door is open: in Seville he meets the ultraist poets around the magazine, Isaac del Vando-Villar among them, and hears for the first time the manifesto language of a Spanish avant-garde hungry to break with the past.
suggested_refs: Grecia magazine, Seville, 31 December 1919 issue, first printing of a Borges poem
sources: infobae.com, 'El primer poema que Borges publicó y que después destruyó'
Carlos Cortínez, 'Himno del mar: el primer poema de Borges'

stops.name: Madrid, the tertulia of the Café Colonial
stops.campa: In Madrid the family finds Rafael Cansinos-Assens, who presides every Saturday past midnight over a tertulia at the Café Colonial that runs until dawn: poets, translators, unclassifiable men of letters, and at the center this one, who has translated the Thousand and One Nights, the Talmud, and the Zohar into Spanish and speaks of Kabbalah and Sufi poetry with the same unhurried authority he gives to French symbolism. Borges, not yet twenty-one, sits at the edge of the circle and listens. Here, before he has read a line of scholarship on Attar or Ibn Arabi, he first hears their names spoken as living doctrine, not dead footnote.
stops.quote: There the great event to me was my friendship with Rafael Cansinos-Asséns... I still like to think of myself as his disciple.
stops.quote_source: An Autobiographical Essay, The New Yorker, 1970 (written in English)
suggested_refs: The Café Colonial, Madrid, site of Cansinos-Assens's Saturday tertulia
sources: visavis.com.ar, 'Rafael Cansinos Assens: el poeta judío español amigo de Borges'
Jorge Schwartz, 'Cansinos Assens y Borges: ¿un vínculo (anti)vanguardista?'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the return on the Reina Victoria
stops.campa: After a second turn through Mallorca and a last season in Madrid signing ultraist manifestos with Guillermo de Torre and the others of the Colonial, the family sails home. Borges disembarks a convinced avant-gardist, twenty-one years old, carrying in his trunk the beginnings of everything: Whitman's line broken into Spanish free verse, Schopenhauer's pessimism, Cansinos-Assens's Kabbalah, and a case of unpublished poems about a city he has been away from for seven years and now must learn to see for the first time as a grown man, and as a subject for poetry rather than a memory.
suggested_refs: The steamship Reina Victoria Eugenia, the family's homeward crossing, March 1921

segments.name: Buenos Aires, the Mythology of the Suburb

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the mural magazine Prisma
stops.campa: With a handful of young poets Borges launches Prisma, a single broadsheet of verse meant not for a magazine stand but for a wall: he and his friends go out at night with paste-buckets and glue it to the fences and construction hoardings of Buenos Aires, an ultraism meant to be read standing in the street. He writes his own manifesto for a poetry of the outlying barrios, the arrabal, rather than the fashionable center, and begins the long labor of remaking Buenos Aires — its low houses, its corner stores, its patios — into a mythology equal to the one he has just left behind in Europe.
suggested_refs: Prisma, mural magazine no. 1, pasted to walls in Buenos Aires, December 1921
sources: estandarte.com, 'Jorge Luis Borges, en diez fechas'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Fervor de Buenos Aires
stops.campa: At his father's expense, three hundred unnumbered copies of Fervor de Buenos Aires come off the press of the Imprenta Serantes, his sister Norah's woodcut on the cover, no price on the wrapper: Borges and his friends leave copies in overcoat pockets at the Sur cafés and slide them under the doors of people whose opinion he wants. The city of low roofs, cemeteries, and long red sunsets is set down for the first time in the plain, exact free verse he has carried back from Europe. He sails for Europe again within a week of the printing, leaving Buenos Aires a book it did not know it needed.
suggested_refs: Fervor de Buenos Aires (Imprenta Serantes, 1923), 300 copies, cover woodcut by Norah Borges
sources: revistaneri.com, 'Fervor de Buenos Aires: a 100 años del primer poemario de Borges'

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo — the founding of Sur
stops.campa: Victoria Ocampo launches Sur from her house in San Isidro, a review meant to open Argentina onto world letters and the world onto Argentina — Ortega y Gasset, Waldo Frank, and Drieu la Rochelle among its early advisory names. Borges joins the circle from its first issues, translating Woolf and Kafka for its pages, publishing there the essays and fictions that will define him. It is not yet the house where he will meet the friend of his life, but it is already the room, the review, and the patroness that will make that meeting, and most of what follows, possible.
suggested_refs: Sur magazine no. 1, January 1931, founded by Victoria Ocampo
sources: Estudios ITAM, 'Jorge Luis Borges en la revista Sur'

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo — meeting Bioy Casares
stops.campa: At a lunch in Victoria Ocampo's house Borges meets Adolfo Bioy Casares, seventeen years younger, tall, elegant, already a published novelist: the two withdraw from the other guests to talk and are scolded by their hostess for the rudeness, which only cements the friendship on the spot, and they leave together for the city. From this afternoon grows a partnership of four decades — joint pseudonyms, joint detective stories, a joint anthology of fantastic literature — and the friend to whom, more than any other, Borges will read a new page before anyone else sees it.
suggested_refs: Villa Ocampo, San Isidro, where Borges and Bioy Casares first met, 1932

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "Una vindicación de la Cábala"
stops.campa: In the essay collection Discusión, Borges takes up the hermeneutic machinery of the Kabbalists he first heard named at the Café Colonial: he does not defend their doctrine of a text with no arbitrary syllable, every letter charged and countable, but the cryptographic method itself, which he calls among the strictest and most fantastic literary criticism ever practiced. He names Gershom Scholem, whom he has not yet met, as its living authority. Philosophy and theology, he writes, are branches of the literature of the fantastic — a sentence that will govern his fiction for the next thirty years.
stops.quote: No quiero vindicar la doctrina, sino los procedimientos hermenéuticos o criptográficos que a ella conducen.
stops.quote_source: Una vindicación de la Cábala (first published 1931), in Discusión (1932)
suggested_refs: Discusión (1932), the essay collection containing 'Una vindicación de la Cábala'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "El acercamiento a Almotásim"
stops.campa: Disguised as a review of a novel that does not exist, "El acercamiento a Almotásim" opens Borges's own door onto the Sufi shelf: the review's fictitious plot, a law student's search through the underworld of Bombay for a man he glimpses only by the goodness his presence leaves in others, is confessed in the essay's own closing note to derive from Farid al-Din Attar's Conference of the Birds, in which thirty birds cross seven valleys to find the Simurgh and find, on the summit, that they themselves compose it. The trick of the false review becomes the mold for every fiction he writes for the next decade.
suggested_refs: Farid al-Din Attar's Mantiq al-Tayr (Conference of the Birds), the source Borges names in the essay's closing note
sources: El acercamiento a Almotásim, in Historia de la eternidad (1936) and later Ficciones

stops.name: Boedo, the Biblioteca Municipal Miguel Cané
stops.campa: Family money thinning after his father's retirement, Borges takes a post cataloguing books at the modest Miguel Cané municipal library in the working-class barrio of Boedo, poorly paid for work no one much wants. The other clerks, he will recall, spend the working day discussing football and boxing in the basement while he finishes an entire day's quota of cataloguing within the first hour and reads or writes fiction in a corner for the rest of it, hidden, he believes, from everyone; only years later does he learn that a fellow clerk had listed him in the telephone directory under a false name, ashamed of the association with a poet.
suggested_refs: The Biblioteca Municipal Miguel Cané, Carlos Calvo 4319, Boedo, Buenos Aires
sources: lanacion.com.ar, 'Los años desconocidos, grises y luminosos de Borges en la biblioteca Miguel Cané'

segments.name: The Wound, the Labyrinth, and the Tyranny

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the accident on the stairs
stops.campa: Running up a dark stairway on Christmas Eve, Borges catches his head on the freshly painted edge of an open casement window; the wound seems slight, but within days a fever rises, and for weeks he lies between septicemia and death, hallucinating, and, more than the fever itself, fearing for his own mind — that if he recovers his body he may not recover his intellect. He tests himself by trying to write something wholly unlike anything he has written before, to see if the faculty of invention has survived intact. The story that comes, when he finally can hold a pen, is "Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote."
suggested_refs: The stairwell accident, Christmas Eve 1938, the hinge between the poet and the fabulist
sources: infobae.com, 'Una corrida por la escalera... la Nochebuena que Borges casi se mata'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "Pierre Menard, autor del Quijote"
stops.campa: Sur publishes, in May, the story Borges wrote to prove to himself that his mind had survived the fever: a French symbolist who sets out not to copy but to independently re-arrive, word for word, at several chapters of Don Quixote, and succeeds, so that identical pages carry different meanings written three centuries apart by different men. It is the first work in what will be called, for want of a better word, Borgesian: fiction disguised as literary criticism, criticism disguised as metaphysics, and behind both the same procedure discovered a few years earlier over the false review of Almotásim.
stops.quote: El texto de Cervantes y el de Menard son verbalmente idénticos, pero el segundo es casi infinitamente más rico.
stops.quote_source: Pierre Menard, autor del Quijote, Sur, May 1939
suggested_refs: Sur magazine, May 1939 issue, first printing of 'Pierre Menard, autor del Quijote'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius"
stops.campa: Sur prints the story of an encyclopedia entry for a country that does not exist, and of the slow, conspiratorial invasion of the real world by the wholly invented idealist planet of Tlön, whose objects duplicate themselves through grief and whose languages have no nouns, only verbs and clusters of adjectives. Borges signs it with the fiction of an editorial footnote reporting his own authorship, blurring, as the Kabbalists blurred the line between commentary and revelation, the boundary between the essay and the world it describes. Bioy Casares walks on in the opening paragraph, remembering the heresiarch who called mirrors and copulation abominable.
stops.quote: Debo a la conjunción de un espejo y de una enciclopedia el descubrimiento de Uqbar.
stops.quote_source: Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius, Sur, May 1940 (opening sentence)
suggested_refs: Sur magazine, May 1940 issue, first printing of 'Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan
stops.campa: His first book of fiction proper gathers eight stories including "La biblioteca de Babel," the universe imagined as an infinite honeycomb of hexagonal galleries holding every possible book, most of them meaningless, a handful of them the exact catalogue and refutation of all the others; and the title story, a Chinese spy's labyrinth-novel in which time itself forks at every choice into simultaneous, incompatible futures. The book sells poorly and loses that year's National Prize for Literature to a work no one now remembers; a jury member later calls the decision, publicly, an outrage. The forking garden becomes, from this printing on, the single most quoted figure in his name.
stops.quote: El universo (que otros llaman la Biblioteca) se compone de un número indefinido, y tal vez infinito, de galerías hexagonales.
stops.quote_source: La biblioteca de Babel, in El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan (1941)
suggested_refs: El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan (Sur, 1941), first edition

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "El Aleph"
stops.campa: Sur publishes the story of a point in space, glimpsed on the nineteenth step of a cellar staircase on the fictional Calle Garay, that contains every other point in the universe without superposition or transparency, seen all at once from every angle: the narrator, jealous and grieving over a dead woman named Beatriz, sees in it the whole earth and is undone by the seeing. Borges will later call the device a shameless enough metaphor, and dedicate the story, with real and unrequited feeling, to Estela Canto, for whom he had wanted the world itself as a gift and could offer instead only this one sentence's cosmos.
stops.quote: Vi el populoso mar, vi el alba y la tarde... vi el Aleph, desde todos los puntos, vi en el Aleph la tierra.
suggested_refs: Sur magazine, September 1945 issue, first printing of 'El Aleph'

stops.name: Boedo, the dismissal from the library
stops.campa: Perón's new government, unamused by a writer who has signed manifestos against fascism and made no secret of his contempt for the regime, has him informed that his post at the Miguel Cané library is abolished — and that a position awaits him instead as inspector of poultry and rabbits in the municipal markets. Borges resigns on the spot rather than accept the humiliation, and tells the story for the rest of his life as the clean, absurd shape of the whole Peronist decade: not imprisonment, not exile, but a small, exact, unforgettable insult, delivered with a bureaucrat's straight face.
suggested_refs: The rectangular sign naming Borges 'inspector of poultry and rabbits,' Central Market, Buenos Aires
sources: infobae.com, 'Borges y Perón: el duelo que comenzó en una biblioteca'
perfil.com, 'Borges, inspector de aves y detective'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "El Simurgh y el águila"
stops.campa: La Nación prints an essay pairing two symbolic birds across three centuries: Dante's eagle of the just kings in Paradiso, formed of a thousand righteous souls speaking with a single voice, and Attar's Simurgh, a century earlier, composed of thirty birds who climb seven valleys of the Sufi path only to discover, on the last mountain, that the bird they sought was themselves multiplied and made one. Borges judges the Persian figure to have quietly corrected and surpassed the Florentine's: Dante's eagle keeps its souls distinct within the sign, while Attar's birds dissolve entirely into the thing they sought. It becomes, decades later, the title piece of Nueve ensayos dantescos.
stops.quote: Treinta, purificados por los trabajos, pisan la montaña del Simurgh. La contemplan al fin; perciben que ellos son el Simurgh y que el Simurgh es cada uno de ellos y todos.
stops.quote_source: El Simurgh y el águila, La Nación, 14 March 1948; collected in Nueve ensayos dantescos (1982)
suggested_refs: Farid al-Din Attar's Mantiq al-Tayr and Dante's eagle of Paradiso XIX-XX, paired in Borges's essay

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the presidency of SADE
stops.campa: Elected president of the Sociedad Argentina de Escritores, Borges turns the writers' guild into one of the few remaining public platforms for open dissent from Peronism, hosting talks and readings the government watches with open suspicion. He is by his own account no organizer and no orator, and leans on friends to manage what the office requires; what he will not do is soften the position. Police visit SADE's rooms more than once during his term to note who is present. He holds the post through the regime's hardest years of censorship and leaves it only when the Society itself, exhausted, can no longer safely meet.
suggested_refs: The Sociedad Argentina de Escritores (SADE), a center of literary resistance to Peronism, 1950-1953
sources: lanacion.com.ar, 'Jorge Luis Borges: las razones de un antiperonismo feroz'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "El escritor argentino y la tradición"
stops.campa: Before the Colegio Libre de Estudios Superiores, Borges delivers the lecture that will outlast most of his fiction as a statement of doctrine: against both the nationalists who demand gauchos and local color and the cosmopolitans who demand only Europe, he argues that Argentines, like Jews within Western culture and Irishmen within English letters, stand close enough to a tradition to use it with reverence and far enough outside it to innovate within it without anxiety. The whole of Western culture, he says, is the Argentine writer's patrimony, to be handled boldly, not timidly imitated. Sixty-five students hear it; it will be read by everyone after.
stops.quote: Creo que nuestra tradición es toda la cultura occidental, y creo también que tenemos derecho a esta tradición, mayor que el que pueden tener los habitantes de una u otra nación occidental.
stops.quote_source: El escritor argentino y la tradición, lecture of 19 December 1951, published 1953
suggested_refs: The Colegio Libre de Estudios Superiores, Buenos Aires, site of the 1951 lecture
Martín Fierro, the gauchesque epic Borges defends and reclaims in the lecture
sources: geografiavirtual.com, 'Borges: El escritor argentino y la tradición'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Director of the Biblioteca Nacional
stops.campa: Weeks after Perón's fall, the new government names Borges director of the National Library, the post once held by his own literary hero Paul Groussac, another blind librarian before him. He accepts a paradise he can no longer read: nine hundred thousand volumes in every language he prizes, and eyes that can no longer make out the spines. He will govern the library for eighteen years by memory, dictation, and the reading of others, walking its shelves by touch and by the maps of it he keeps entirely in his head, more possessive of its geography, staff will say, than any sighted director before him.
stops.quote: Yo siempre me había imaginado el Paraíso bajo la especie de una biblioteca.
stops.quote_source: La ceguera, in Siete Noches (1980), lecture of 1977, recalling the appointment of 1955
suggested_refs: The old Biblioteca Nacional building, Calle México 564, Buenos Aires, Borges's directorship 1955-1973
sources: cadena3.com, 'Cómo hizo Jorge Luis Borges para transformar su ceguera en un don'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "Poema de los dones"
stops.campa: In the library that is now entirely his and entirely closed to him by sight, Borges composes the poem that will become the emblem of the whole irony: no one, he writes, should reduce to tears or reproach this declaration of the mastery of a God who, with magnificent irony, granted him at the same time the books and the night. He does not mean the line as complaint; he means it, and will go on meaning it for thirty more years, as a description of an exchange that on balance he does not regret, since the night has proven, in its own way, generous.
stops.quote: Nadie rebaje a lágrima o reproche esta declaración de la maestría de Dios que con magnífica ironía me dio a la vez los libros y la noche.
stops.quote_source: Poema de los dones (1955), in El hacedor (1960)
suggested_refs: Poema de los dones, written on assuming the directorship of the Biblioteca Nacional

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the study of Old English and Old Norse
stops.campa: Unable to read new books by his own eyes, Borges turns his blindness toward a language no living tongue can spoil for him: Old English, then Old Norse, the tongues of the Völsunga Saga his father gave him at ten years old and of the Beowulf poet he has loved since Geneva. He gathers a handful of students at his apartment on Calle Maipú one evening a week — not a class, he insists, but a shared discovery, since he can read the grammar no better than they — and works through the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and the Eddas by ear, dictation, and the slow triumph of memorized declension.
suggested_refs: The Völsunga Saga, given to Borges by his father at age ten, seed of a lifelong study
sources: dialnet.unirioja.es, 'Borges y la literatura islandesa medieval'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "El Golem"
stops.campa: He composes the poem that returns, twenty-six years after the essay in Discusión, to the Prague legend he first met as a German novel in Geneva: a rabbi who, following the letter-combinations of the Kabbalists, animates a shapeless creature of clay, only to find a grey golem that sweeps the temple and understands nothing of the mystical machinery that made it. Borges reads in the story his own oldest joke against himself — the maker who cannot fully account for, or control, what the maker makes — and closes with a final stanza in which God, too, must look with something like pity on His own imperfect golem: man.
stops.quote: El rabí lo miraba con ternura / y con algún horror. ¿Cómo (se dijo) / pude engendrar este penoso hijo / y la inacción dejé, que es la cordura?
stops.quote_source: El Golem, composed 1958; collected in El otro, el mismo (1964)
suggested_refs: Gustav Meyrink's Der Golem, read in Geneva forty years earlier, closing the circle
sources: scielo.cl, 'Paradoja y deconstrucción en El golem de Jorge Luis Borges'

stops.name: Formentor, Mallorca — the International Publishers' Prize
stops.campa: On the same island where, forty-two years before, a nineteen-year-old had drafted paper manifestos with Jacobo Sureda, the jury of the Prix International des Éditeurs, meeting at the Hotel Formentor, names Jorge Luis Borges co-winner of its first prize, sharing the honor with Samuel Beckett. The award, more than any single book, is what turns a name known mainly to readers of Sur into a name translated within two years into English, French, Italian, and German, and read by writers on every continent who had never before heard of Buenos Aires. He will call the years after Formentor his second, unearned, and entirely unexpected career.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Formentor, Mallorca, where Borges and Beckett shared the first Prix International des Éditeurs

segments.name: The World Lecture Circuit and the Dante-Islam Door

stops.name: Buenos Aires, marriage to Elsa Astete Millán
stops.campa: At sixty-seven, prompted in part by his mother's wish to see him settled before she died, Borges marries Elsa Astete Millán, a widow he had courted decades before as a young man. The marriage is unhappy almost from its first months — she has little patience for the parade of foreign visitors and the endless dictation his blindness requires, and he finds himself, by his own later account, ill-suited to the ordinary machinery of a shared household after a lifetime organized entirely around his mother, his books, and his work. They separate within three years; Argentina's law of the day allows no clean divorce, only a civil separation.
suggested_refs: Elsa Astete Millán, whom Borges married in 1967 and separated from in 1970

stops.name: Cambridge, Massachusetts — the Norton Lectures
stops.campa: Harvard names Borges to the Charles Eliot Norton chair of poetry, and across the fall and following spring he delivers, in English, without notes, six lectures — on the riddle of poetry, on metaphor, on the telling of a tale, on word-music and translation, on his own poetic creed — that ramble by design across the whole of world literature: the Eddas, Whitman, the kenningar of the Icelandic skalds, Dante, the Anglo-Saxon riddles. The tapes are shelved unpublished for thirty years and rediscovered, transcribed, only after his death, but the visiting American writers who hear him live carry the name Borges home to a country still mostly unaware of him.
stops.quote: I am nearing seventy. I have given the major part of my life to literature, and I can offer you only doubts.
stops.quote_source: The Riddle of Poetry, first Charles Eliot Norton Lecture, Harvard, 1967
suggested_refs: This Craft of Verse, the six Norton Lectures, recorded 1967-68 and published posthumously in 2000

stops.name: Reykjavík, Iceland — the first crossing
stops.campa: The lifelong reader of the Eddas and the sagas at last sets foot in Iceland itself, sixty years after his father first put the Völsunga Saga into a ten-year-old's hands in Buenos Aires. He cannot see the volcanic fields or the northern light he has imagined for six decades from books, but he can, with a half-memorized dictionary, follow spoken Icelandic on the street, and he is visibly, uncharacteristically moved simply by the fact of being there, in the country whose medieval prose he considers a wonder the rest of Europe still underrates. He will return twice more before he dies.
stops.quote: Cuando llegué a Islandia, me sentí conmovido. Me emocionó el mero hecho de estar en Islandia.
stops.quote_source: Borges on his first visit to Iceland (1971), cited in La Nación, 'La Islandia de Borges'
suggested_refs: The Icelandic sagas and Eddas, subject of Borges's Las kenningar (1933) and Literaturas germánicas medievales (1966)
sources: dialnet.unirioja.es, 'Borges y la literatura islandesa medieval'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Teatro Coliseo — the night of the Thousand and One Nights
stops.campa: In one of the seven public lectures later collected as Siete Noches, Borges takes as his subject the book his father's own library first gave him as a boy and that Cansinos-Assens, in Madrid, had made his own life's translation labor: the Thousand and One Nights. He tells the crowded Coliseo that the book is not dead literature but an inexhaustible one, that its title alone — a thousand and one, not a round thousand — already suggests infinity, and that a reader can enter Burton's, Galland's, Lane's, or Mardrus's very different Nights and each time find, honestly, a different and equally real book.
stops.quote: Las mil y una noches no han muerto. El infinito tiempo de Las mil y una noches prosigue su camino.
stops.quote_source: Las mil y una noches, in Siete Noches (1980), lecture of 1977
suggested_refs: The Burton, Galland, Lane, and Mardrus translations of the Thousand and One Nights, compared by Borges since 1935's 'Los traductores de las 1001 Noches'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Teatro Coliseo — the night of the Kabbalah
stops.campa: A later night of the same cycle returns Borges, forty-five years after Discusión, to the subject Cansinos-Assens first opened to him: he tells the Coliseo that the Kabbalists read the Torah as a text in which no letter is accidental, in which the whole future and the whole past lie already encrypted in the exact wording God chose — a book that is also a cipher of the universe, and the universe read, in turn, as a book. He does not defend the doctrine; he defends, once more, the beauty of the method.
stops.quote: El curioso modus operandi de los cabalistas está basado en una premisa lógica: la idea de que la Escritura es un texto absoluto, y en un texto absoluto nada puede ser obra del azar.
stops.quote_source: La Cábala, in Siete Noches (1980), lecture of 1977
suggested_refs: Siete Noches, the seven public lectures at the Teatro Coliseo, Buenos Aires, June-August 1977

stops.name: Alcalá de Henares — the Cervantes Prize
stops.campa: On the day of Saint George and of Cervantes's own death, King Juan Carlos hands Borges, sharing the honor that year with the Spanish poet Gerardo Diego, the Premio Cervantes in the great hall of the University of Alcalá — the highest prize the Spanish language gives itself, awarded at last to the writer of Pierre Menard, whose whole youth-long argument with and inside the Quixote is thereby, without anyone quite saying so, ratified by the language's own governing academies. Borges, entirely blind for a quarter century now, is led to the podium and gives thanks in the same unhurried, precise prose that has not altered in fifty years.
suggested_refs: The Paraninfo of the University of Alcalá de Henares, site of the Cervantes Prize ceremony

stops.name: Madrid, Nueve ensayos dantescos
stops.campa: Espasa-Calpe gathers into a single volume nine essays on the Divine Comedy written across four decades, among them the 1948 pairing of Dante's eagle with Attar's Simurgh, now given the whole book's title. Borges, dictating the preface at eighty-two, reasserts a claim he has held since Cansinos-Assens's tertulia: that the medieval Islamic mystics, and Ibn Arabi's account of Muhammad's night ascension above all, as Miguel Asín Palacios had first argued in 1919, stand as plausible tributaries feeding Dante's own architecture of the other world, whether or not the Florentine ever read a word of Arabic. The book closes, deliberately, the circle opened sixty years earlier in a Madrid café.
suggested_refs: Miguel Asín Palacios, La escatología musulmana en la Divina Comedia (1919), and Ibn Arabi's account of the Mi'raj
sources: americanistas.es, 'Pensamiento y parodia en las páginas dantescas de Borges'

stops.name: Asunción, Paraguay — marriage to María Kodama
stops.campa: Since Argentina's law still permits no clean divorce from Elsa, Borges and María Kodama — his student, his travelling companion and reader for two decades, his literary executor since 1979 — marry by proxy in a civil ceremony across the river in Asunción, where Paraguayan law allows what Buenos Aires does not. He is eighty-six and dying of the liver cancer diagnosed months before; the marriage is, among other things, a last act of order, settling into a single name the estate of the whole invented and actual life: every manuscript, every right, every future edition, entrusted now formally to the last of his readers.
suggested_refs: The civil registry of Asunción, Paraguay, site of the proxy marriage of 26 April 1986
sources: batimes.com.ar, 'María Kodama, widow of Jorge Luis Borges, dies at 86'

segments.name: Geneva, the Return and the Grave

stops.name: Geneva, the death
stops.campa: Borges dies in Geneva on the fourteenth of June, in the city he chose deliberately, at the end, over Buenos Aires — fearing, he had told friends, that a death at home would be made into a national circus. He is the boy who arrived here in 1914 not meaning to stay a week past the season, who took his baccalauréat in this town and met his first German grammar and his first Schopenhauer here; now, at eighty-six, he closes the circle: Geneva first and Geneva last, with fifty years of Buenos Aires folded between. The funeral leaves four days later from the Cathedral of Saint Peter.
suggested_refs: Geneva, chosen deliberately by Borges as the place to die, June 1986
sources: infobae.com, 'Los misterios de la lápida de Borges'

stops.name: Geneva, Cimetière de Plainpalais
stops.campa: María Kodama commissions a gravestone for the Cimetière des Rois that reads Borges's own private mythology back at the visitor in stone: on its face, seven Anglo-Saxon warriors raise broken swords in relief, defeated, beneath the Old English line "And ne forhtedon na" from The Battle of Maldon — be not afraid; on its reverse, a Viking longship and a line drawn from the twenty-seventh chapter of the Volsunga Saga. No Spanish appears anywhere on the stone. The library that was Paradise, the Simurgh, the Kabbalists' cipher, the sagas learned by ear in blindness — all of it converges on two dead northern languages carved over Argentine bones.
suggested_refs: The gravestone of Jorge Luis Borges, Cimetière de Plainpalais (Cimetière des Rois), Geneva, designed by María Kodama
sources: infobae.com, 'Los misterios de la lápida de Borges'
